titre: The Twelve Tables: Rome's Law That Was Never Found Again
accroche: Around 450-449 BCE, Rome inscribed its law for the first time. No fragment of it has survived: we know it only through the schoolboys who learned it by heart.
contenu_vulgarise:
In front of the Curia, in the Roman Forum, twelve tables were fixed to the Rostra. Livy says they were bronze; Pomponius says ivory: on this point the sources disagree. What matters is that any Roman could now stop in front of them and read, with their own eyes, the rules that governed them. Before 449 BCE, this law existed, but only the pontiffs, all patricians, knew it and interpreted it, case by case, to their own order's advantage.

## A concession won by leaving

Since the Republic's founding in 509 BCE, only patricians could hold a magistracy. The plebeians, who made up Rome's workforce, held a formidable weapon: secession, mass withdrawal from the city, which paralyzed the Roman economy. It was through this means that they won, according to the tradition reported by Wikipedia, the codification of a law that had until then remained largely customary. A first board of ten men, the decemvirs, drafted ten tables in 451 BCE. Livy recounts that an embassy was supposedly sent to Greece to study Solon's constitution in Athens; modern historians doubt this, leaning instead toward contact with the Greek cities of southern Italy. A second decemvirate added two more tables in 450, and a fresh plebeian secession then forced the Senate to have the whole text adopted by the centuriate assembly in 449.

## What the text says, and what it does not change

The Avalon Project's translation (Yale Law School) gives a sense of the content. Table VIII distinguishes a thief caught at night, whom the owner may lawfully kill on the spot, from one caught by day unarmed, who is whipped and handed over into bondage to his victim. Table V keeps women under guardianship even as adults, on account of their "levity of mind," except for the Vestals. Table X limits funeral expenses, down to the number of mourners and flute players allowed. These rules were now readable by anyone, but they were not, for that, any kinder to the plebeians: the same law, in Table XI, forbade them from marrying a patrician. Writing the law down did not make it fairer. It only stopped being the secret of a single order.

The real shift lies elsewhere. The Twelve Tables themselves did not survive: no fragment, original or copied, has come down to us. According to Paul R. Coleman-Norton's edition, they were most likely destroyed when Rome was sacked by the Gauls, in 387 BCE. Everything we know of them comes from quotations made by later writers. Cicero, in his treatise *De Legibus* (II, 23, 59), recounts that the schoolboys of his childhood still learned the Twelve Tables by heart, "ut carmen necessarium," like a chant they had to know. The first Roman law written down so that everyone could read it without an intermediary has thus reached us only through schoolboys' memory, relayed by other books: the engraved text is gone; the recitation crossed the centuries.

carte.punch: Around 449 BCE, Rome inscribed its first written law. No fragment of it was ever found again.
carte.idee: The Twelve Tables, the first Roman law put in writing around 450-449 BCE, survive today in no physical form. We know them only through later writers' quotations, including Cicero, who recounts having had to learn them by heart as a boy, like a required chant.

quiz.question: Why did the plebeians win, around 450-449 BCE, the writing-down of Roman law?
choix: So the law would stop being the secret of the patrician pontiffs, who interpreted it to their own advantage
To abolish the distinction between patricians and plebeians
To replace Rome's magistracies with a single tribunal
So Rome would directly adopt Solon's laws, as passed in Athens
quiz.explication: Before the Twelve Tables, Roman law remained customary and known only to the patrician pontiffs, who applied it to their own advantage. Writing it down did not abolish the patrician-plebeian distinction, still present in Table XI, touched no magistracy, and did not directly adopt Solon's laws: the embassy to Greece reported by Livy is itself doubted.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What remains today of the Twelve Tables' original text?
choix: No fragment, original or copied: the text is known only through later writers' quotations
The first ten tables, engraved in bronze, kept at the Roman Forum
A complete copy found in the archives of the Capitoline Hill
Only Table XI, on the ban on intermarriage between orders, has been recovered
quiz_supplementaire.explication: No fragment of the Twelve Tables, original or copied, has survived: they were likely destroyed when Rome was sacked by the Gauls in 387 BCE. Everything known of them comes from quotations by later writers, including Cicero.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Cicero (De Legibus, II, 23, 59), how did the schoolboys of his childhood learn the Twelve Tables?
choix: By heart, like a chant they had to know ("ut carmen necessarium")
By each copying out every table by hand onto a wax tablet
By attending their public recitation at the Forum every year
They did not learn them: only future pontiffs studied them
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Cicero recounts that, in his childhood, schoolboys had to learn the Twelve Tables by heart, "ut carmen necessarium," like a required chant. Nothing in the sources mentions an individual handwritten copy, an annual public recitation, or a reservation to future pontiffs.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the tradition reported by Livy, what did the decemvirs supposedly do before drafting the Twelve Tables?
choix: Send an embassy to Greece to study Solon's constitution
Consult the patrician pontiffs, who would have drafted the text instead
Convene an assembly of plebeians to dictate the law themselves
Take over the existing customary law without any change
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Livy reports that an embassy was supposedly sent to Greece to study Solon's constitution in Athens, an account modern historians doubt, leaning instead toward contact with the Greek cities of southern Italy. Nothing points to drafting by the pontiffs, by the plebeians themselves, or a plain repeat of existing customary law.
